title: Gerrit Graham, Actor in ‘Phantom of the Paradise,’ Screenwriter and Grateful Dead Collaborator, Dies at 77
description: Gerrit Graham, an actor, screenwriter and songwriter who co-wrote a song for The Grateful Dead, died on Tuesday in Rhinebeck, N.Y. He was 77. He suf
body:
Gerrit Graham, an actor, screenwriter and songwriter who co-wrote a song for The Grateful Dead, died on Tuesday in Rhinebeck, N.Y. He was 77. He suffered from lung disease, among other ailments.

	Graham began his career starring alongside Robert De Niro in early Brian de Palma films “Hi Mom!” and “Greetings,” later appearing in films such as “Demon Seed,” “Pretty Baby,” “Child’s Play 2” and “National Lampoon’s Class Reunion.” Skilled in impressions and accents, Graham also appeared in episodes of “Seinfeld,” “Laverne and Shirley” and “The Wonder Years,” and on both “Star Trek: Deep Space Nine” and “Star Trek: Voyager.”
	

	He played the glam rocker Beef, who is unveiled in a coffin and silenced in the shower with a plunger, in de Palma’s “Phantom of the Paradise,” and a sleazy used car salesman in Robert Zemeckis’ “Used Cars.”


	As a screenwriter, Graham worked on projects including “The Little Mermaid,” “Oliver & Company” and episodes of “The Twilight Zone.” He co-wrote the Disney adaptation of “Prince and The Pauper” alongside his brother, Chris Hubbell. Also a songwriter and lyricist, Graham most notably collaborated with Bob Weir of The Grateful Dead. They co-wrote “Victim or The Crime,” which was recorded by the band for their “Built To Last” album and later by Weir and Rob Wasserman on their 1998 “Live” album.

	Graham was born in New York City to parents John and Janet, and the family went on to live in Missouri and Michigan before settling in Chicago. In 1982, he married his wife, Deborah, with whom he had two children. He previously served on the Burger Hill Preservation Society while living in Rhinebeck, N.Y., for the last 30 years of his life after caring for his mother in California.
	

	Graham is survived by his brother, Sam; his sons, Jack and Henry, and their wives, Talia and Joelle; and his four grandchildren, Nolan, Micah, Vera and Joey.

title: Gaza Documentary ‘NAZA’ Sets U.S. Theatrical Release Through Self-Distribution Model
description: “NAZA,” the acclaimed and controversial documentary about killings in Gaza, has set a distribution rollout for U.S. theaters starting Sept. 30 via a
body:
“NAZA,” the acclaimed and controversial documentary about killings in Gaza, has set a distribution rollout for U.S. theaters starting Sept. 30 via an innovative plan that forgoes selling the film to a studio or independent distributor.

	The rollout, which kicks off exclusively at the IFC Center in New York City, is “spearheaded by The Guardian and mk2, who have assembled a team of U.S. and international partners and consultants to bring the film to audiences as quickly as possible,” according to a release.
	

	The documentary will expand to Los Angeles and other markets on Oct. 9 and then roll out nationally. 


	It’s looking like a busy fall for theatrical releases of documentaries: buzzy nonfiction titles set for October openings include Alex Gibney’s “Musk” on Oct. 9 and Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes doc “You Can See Everything” on Oct. 16.

	Directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the two Israeli directors of the Oscar-winning documentary “No Other Land,” “NAZA” won a special jury prize at the recent Venice Film Festival. Its North American premiere is at The New York Film Festival on Sept. 26. 

	“No Other Land” was released in the U.S. through Cinetic with bookings by Michael Tuckman Media rather than using a traditional distributor.

	Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, “NAZA” reveals in detail the systems behind “Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to the synopsis. NAZA is the military acronym used by Israeli intelligence to describe the number of civilians it expects will be killed in an airstrike.
	

	Directors Abraham and Szor said in a statement, “We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli filmmakers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible. While filming members of Israel’s military on rooftops at night in Tel Aviv over the past three years, we found ourselves asking the very questions that were asked by our grandparents’ generation and throughout the 20th century: how does one group of people allow the total dehumanization of another? What do the inner workings of such a system look like? Many of the revelations in the film were published almost immediately as we learned of them, in the months following the October 7th attacks, by The Guardian (one of NAZA’s producers), in collaboration with reporting partners +972 Magazine and Local Call. The film lets us explore something deeper than we could in our investigative journalism alone: not only the words being said but also those that are not said, the silence. It is up to all of us to break that silence.”

	“NAZA” is produced by The Guardian and James Wilson (JW Films) and executive produced by Jonathan Glazer.

schema.headline: Gaza Documentary ‘NAZA’ Sets U.S. Theatrical Release Through Self-Distribution Model

title: Getting to Know Juan Andrés García Ropero ‘Bropi,’ the New Director of Content of Movistar Plus
description:
Juan Andrés García Ropero, “Bropi,” Movistar Plus’ new director of content from May 2026, re-adjusts himself in his seat on a Zoom call.

	“I’ll sit
body:
Juan Andrés García Ropero, “Bropi,” Movistar Plus’ new director of content from May 2026, re-adjusts himself in his seat on a Zoom call.

	“I’ll sit with my best side showing, this profile,” he jokes. For an executive in one of the most pressured jobs in Spain, whom its film and TV industry desperately hope it will continue to invest in movies and shows with an ambition which has yielded “Querer,” “The New Years” and “The Anatomy of a Moment” in TV and “Sirat,” “The Beloved” and “La Bola Negra” in movies, García Ropero seems remarkably relaxed.
	

	He does, however, have good reason. When Variety interviewed García Ropero in late July, he already had on his hands not so much a feature as a movie phenomenon.


	Recipient of a 16-minute standing ovation and a shared best director award at Cannes, queer epic “La Bola Negra” reflects the extraordinary aspirations of not only writer-director-producers Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi but also producer Movistar Plus, the biggest Spanish pay TV/SVOD operator.

	Those ambitions even two months ago were scaling globally. Netflix had set a 47-day U.S. theatrical window for “La Bola Negra” the longest for any movie in the streaming giant’s history, as the film also appears to feature among the streamer’s awards priorities for the fall.

	That breakout success is part of larger traction. In a bigger picture, over 2025-26, apart from France, no country in the world apart, not even the U.S., has had more Cannes main competition contenders than Spain.

	Three of the five movies are Movistar Plus originals: Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s “The Beloved,” starring Javier Bardem, “La Bola Negra” and 2025’s “Sirāt,” a two-time Oscar nominee and Cannes Jury Prize winner. A fourth, Pedro Almodovar’s “Bitter Christmas,” was the subject of a muscular Movistar Plus pre-buy.
	

	A significant part of the conversation at the 74th edition of Spain’s San Sebastián Film Festival, running Sept. 18-26, looks set to be driven by Movistar Plus does next, the Spanish premiere of “La Bola Negra,” a screening of “The Beloved,” and world premieres of Movistar Plus series “El castillo” and new movie “5 More Minutes.”

	With all three movies screening on Sept. 19, this converts that day into a kind of Movistar Plus Super Saturday.

	‘La Bola Negra’

	Unveiling its first movie slate in January 2024, Movistar Plus talked about creating “event auteur movies.” No Movistar Plus film fits better that description to date than “La Bola Negra.”

	Boasting big stars – Penelope Cruz is an extended cameo performance as a cabaret star rousing and arousing the troops, and Glenn Close as a modern-day Hispanist academic – “La Bola Negra” braids three inter-connected stories of gay identity, desire, repression and legacy set in 1932, 1937 and 2017, shot in 35 mm, each story mixing different film registers. It has big Spanish stars, such as Miguel Bernardeau (“Elite,” “Querer”), an enormous Spanish ensemble, and “the idea of a super production that is auteur-driven but also very queer,” as Ambrossi told Variety.

	“Given its production standards, how it’s shot and told, ‘La Bola Negra’ becomes a great event. It will make a lot of noise in San Sebastian and I’m convinced it will mark a milestone in Spanish cinema, a great success for Movistar Plus and and Los Javis, taking them into another dimension,” says García Ropero.

	Sold out worldwide by Goodfellas, “La bola negra” will see Elastica Films launch its nationwide theatrical release on Sept. 25. On Wednesday, the film was announced as Spain’s Oscar race entry for International Feature.

	‘The Beloved’

	“The Beloved” (“El ser querido”) also features as a 2026 standout Spanish feature. Framing a monumental performance by Javier Bardem as an Oscar-winning director seeking reconciliation with his daughter (Victoria Luengo) casting her in his latest movie, “The Beloved,”a story about the story people tell, even to deceive themselves, drew excellent reviews at Cannes: “Bardem is “a formidable presence, Luengo “exudes a fascinating quality of pensive engagement” in the film’s memorable opening scene.” The Beloved has also grossed €3.0 million ($3.45 million) in Spain from an Aug. 28 bow.
	

	Movistar Plus Strategy Going Forward

	The two films’ roll-out comes just months after the second management shakeup in just over a year at Movistar Plus+ with Daniel Domenjó replaced as CEO by Alfonso Gómez Palacio, to to date head of operations of Movistar Plus+ parent Telefónica in Latin America, outside Brazil. Gómez Palacio has won fame for balancing the books and improving margins. Given that, Spain TV and film industry feared that his appointment woild signal a pull back from production.

	So early July news took the industry by storm: Movistar Plus announced that over the next three years it will double original Spanish series annual output from eight to 16 titles, while adding another 10 titles via co-production and licensing deals.

	In early May, Movistar Plus launched a cut-price Free Plan: Series-Cinema subscription offer at just €4.99 ($5.78) a month

	“We are suddenly seeing promise in (and putting money behind) scaled local streaming services to ‘take on’ the U.S. giants. Arguably Sky/ITV are angling for the same,” says Guy Bisson. “We are at a point in the industry where legacy players (and legacy usually goes hand in hand with geographic footprint limitations) see that they have to scale or die and that is now being reflected in content strategy.”

	“Movistar Plus is still the foremost home for Spanish creativity. We aim to build on that sensation even more with a sense of local ambition, but looking for titles which can have international relevance,” García Ropero tells Variety.

	Justifying the production hike, Movistar Plus noted that “Originals attract more clients and generate more engagement.”

	García Ropero cites the case of YouTube-podcast Victoria Martín’s debut “Many People Need to Die,” a withering take on Millennial angst which has proved to be the most watched series of the year on Movistar Plus. “It’s been an audience and new subscriber driver,” says García Romero, noting that Movistar Plus has already ordered a Season 2.

	Financial website El Confidencial claims that Movistar Plus will now double content investment to €200 million ($232 million) a year. Garcia Ropero declined to comment on exact figures but recognized that the pay TV/streamer will be upping not only content volume but investment. The increased TV show hike indeed guarantees that.
	

	One major key to Netflix and HBO Max growth in international has been their bundling in international markets through partnerships with local distributors, such as HBO Max’s alliance in Germany with RTL+.

	Having insisted on not partnering with rivals in Spain, Movistar Plus has now tapped “Ella maldita alma,” a young Spanish priest romantic melodrama, from Plano a Plano and Mediaset España, “33 days” from Atresmedia; and live audience sitcom “La Casa Nostra,” a hot on Catalan public broadcaster 3Cat, made available on Movistar Plus in either its original Catalan or dubbed into Castilian Spanish.

	“In the final analysis, we’re aiming for clients to find on Movistar Plus what they need,” said García Ropero, noting that buying “33 Days” is a “very natural step,” given that it is a fiction recreation from Carles Porta, already a true crime fixture on Movistar Plus.

	The Spanish streamer’s plans for film production have still to be announced. Their strategy, however, may not differ from series, since Movistar Plus seeks the same effect: Subscribers and fidelity for its pay TV and streaming service.

	“Above all, what we’re trying to do is to bet on the best talent,” not on genres or formats but creators with their own voices,” says García Ropero. “That’s been the policy in recent years and we want to continue.”

	‘El Castillo’

	That can be seen in both “El Castillo” and “5 Minutes More.”

	San Sebastián has become a privileged launchpad for series which go on to glean international renown: 2024 hosted world premieres of “Querer” and “Celeste,” both Movistar Plus+ Original Series, which went on to win the two biggest prizes at 2025’s Series Mania, Europe’s most important TV festival.

	In 2020, one of the received titles, films included, was Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s “Riot Police,” written with Isabel Peña, his career-long co-scribe, and producer-writer Eduardo Villanueva, a partner at Sorogoyen’s label El Caballo Films.

	“[San Sebastián Festival director] Jose Luis Rebordinos is a fan of our series and all of the work over these years to bring cinema talent to elevate our original Spanish fiction series,” says García Ropero.

	Bearing out a creator-driven approach, as in “La Bola Negra,” with “El Castillo” and Movistar Plus+ is looking to take talent to the next level. A six-part series, “El Castillo” marks Peña first series without Sorogoyen, catching Spain’s sex trade as it transforms from small road-side establishments to organized crime.
	

	Told from a triple point of view, part procedural, part personal odyssey of a victim, Colombian Claudia, part the rise – and one suspects fall – of a prostitution kingpin, “El Castillo” looks high on two factors many viewers now look for in a series: Authenticity and relevance.

	“Again, I think “El Castillo” will make a lot noise, prove a conversation driver at San Sebastián,” says Garcia Ropero.

	‘5 More Minutes’

	A top Spanish stand-up comic, “5 More Minutes” writer-actor Berto Romero has risen the ranks at Movistar Plus from with star turns on late nights shows “Buenafuente” and “Leit Motiv,” to a first fiction series, “Look What You’ve Done,” a parenting comedy and then “The Other Side,” a comedic-horror-thriller. “5 More Minutes” delivers another genre mashup, a comedic sci-fi survival thriller as an on-the-rocks couple are caught in time loop at a rural getaway.

	“The Other World,” Season 2 of “The Other Side,” will bow later this year with Romero co-directing for the first time.

	“It’s not easy to blend comedy, horror and parapsychology,” says Romero. “Berto likes this mix of different genres and ‘5 More Minutes’ is a magnificent example.”

schema.headline: Getting to Know Juan Andrés García Ropero ‘Bropi,’ the New Director of Content of Movistar Plus

title: Brad Pitt Returning for ‘World War Z’ Sequel at Paramount With Edward Berger to Direct
description:
Brad Pitt will officially return to star in Paramount’s long-awaited sequel to “World War Z.” 

	“All Quiet on the Western Front” and “Conclave” hel
body:
Brad Pitt will officially return to star in Paramount’s long-awaited sequel to “World War Z.” 

	“All Quiet on the Western Front” and “Conclave” helmer Edward Berger, who recently directed Pitt in “The Riders” for A24, has signed on to direct from a script by Dennis Kelly. Plot details for the sequel are being kept under wraps. 

	Pitt will produce the sequel alongside Dede Gardner and Jeremy Kleiner on behalf of Plan B, with Berger on board as executive producer.
	

	The original “World War Z,” based on Max Brooks’ bestselling 2006 novel, “World War Z: An Oral History of the Zombie War,” made more than $540 million at the global box office. The film, directed by Marc Forster, starred Pitt as Gerry Lane, a former United Nations employee, in a race against time to stop a zombie pandemic. At CinemaCon in April, Paramount announced that a sequel was finally in active development after multiple attempts to get another movie off the ground, including a version from Pitt’s frequent collaborator David Fincher, which was scrapped in 2019.


	The “World War Z” update comes amid Pitt’s press tour for his latest Paramount movie, “Heart of the Beast,” in theaters next Friday. The survival thriller, directed by David Ayer, follows a Special Forces officer and his combat dog who, after a devastating plane crash, get stranded deep in the Alaskan wilderness. Pitt will then reprise his Oscar-winning role in Netflix’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” directed by Fincher from a screenplay by Quentin Tarantino. The movie debuts in Imax theaters globally on Nov. 25, then begins streaming on Dec. 23. Next up is “The Rider,” which Pitt and Berger wrapped filming on earlier this year; the movie is currently in post-production. 
	

	Pitt is represented by CAA and Brillstein Entertainment Partners; Berger is represented by CAA, Range, Casarotto Ramsay & Associates, and Hanson Jacobson; and Kelly is represented by UTA, Casarotto Ramsay & Associates, and Davis Law Group.

	Deadline first reported the update on the sequel’s development.

schema.headline: Brad Pitt Returning for ‘World War Z’ Sequel at Paramount With Edward Berger to Direct

title: TV Operators Power Spain’s Global Breakout as the San Sebastian Film Festival Readies Launch: ‘Spanish Cinema Has Never Been So Powerful’
description: Over the last year or so, Spain has burst onto the world stage, scoring five Cannes main competition berths — more than any other country in the wor
body:
Over the last year or so, Spain has burst onto the world stage, scoring five Cannes main competition berths — more than any other country in the world outside France — with joint best director winner “La Bola Negra” now prominent in awards season conversations. 

	Spain’s San Sebastián Film Festival looks set to capture this momentum and also play a key role in Spain’s global breakout.  


	“I’m 64. I’ve been programming cinema since I was 28. Spanish cinema has never been so powerful, with so many important international films,” says San Sebastían festival director José Luis Rebordinos. 
	

	One reason, Rebordinos says, is the work of Spain’s broadcasters and streamers. This year’s San Sebastián is a case in point. Of pay TV/SVOD services, Movistar Plus, the biggest Spanish operator, has three titles in major sections at San Sebastián: “La Bola Negra,” a Neflix U.S. pickup, “El Castillo” and “5 Minutes More,” and Netflix Spain has one: “After Society.” 

	A Movistar Plus Original like previous Cannes competition contenders “Sirāt” and “The Beloved,” “La Bola Negra” weaves the travails and legacy of Spain’s gay experience in 1932, Spanish Civil War-torn 1937 and 2017, picking up on four pages in an unfinished novel by revered poet-playwright Federico García Lorca. Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi direct. 

	“Above all, what we’re trying to do is to bet on the best talent, not on genres or formats but creators with their own voices,” says Movistar Plus director of contents Juan Andrés García Ropero.
	

	“La Bola Negra” is also a reflection of the extraordinary ambitions of both Movistar Plus and Los Javis — as Calvo and Ambrossi are known in Spain. Its budget has been reported as anywhere between €14 million ($16 million) and €18 million ($20 million), which can only be achieved in Europe via a daring and bullish backing by a major player. 

	Those ambitions are now scaling globally. “La Bola Negra” is already being talked up by awards pundits as a frontrunner to score an international feature nomination, plus possible recognition in other Oscar categories. 

	Netflix, having picked up the U.S. and Canada at Cannes, has set a 47-day U.S. window between theatrical and streaming for “La Bola Negra,” from Oct. 16 to Dec. 1, the longest for any movie in the streaming giant’s history.

	“La Bola Negra’s” screening at San Sebastián, theatrical bow in Spain via Elástica on Sept. 25 and its North American premiere at the Toronto Intl. Film Festival will be a further test of the film’s audience appeal.  

	“Given its production standards, how it’s shot and told, ‘La Bola Negra’ becomes a great event. It will make a lot of noise in San Sebastián and I’m convinced it will mark a milestone in Spanish cinema, a great success for Movistar Plus and and Los Javis, taking them to another dimension,” predicts García Ropero. 

	One large question at this year’s San Sebastián fest is whether six-part Movistar Plus series “El Castillo,” co-created by Isabel Peña, Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s career-long co-scribe, can now take Peña’s career to the next level. 

	“El Castillo” follows Spain’s sex trade as it transforms from small road-side establishments to macro-brothels and nationwide organized crime. It‘s Peña‘’’s first solo outing.  

	Building good word-of-mouth in the run-up to San Sebastián, “El Castillo” weighs in as an authentically tawdry chronicle told from a three viewpoints: sex worker Claudia, a single mother from Colombia, voracious prostitution kingpin Manuel and young inspector Liesa, part of a police special unit determined to bring Manuel down.

	“Again, I think ‘El Castillo’ will make a lot noise and prove a conversation-driver at San Sebastián,” says García Ropero.
	

	Feature “5 More Minutes” also looks like a step-up for writer-actor Berto Romero. A top Spanish standup, he has risen in the Movistar Plus ranks from star turns on late-night shows to a first fiction series, shepherding comedy “Look What You’ve Done,” and then “The Other Side,” a comedic-horror-thriller. 

	In comedic sci-fi thriller “5 More Minutes” an on-the-rocks couple are caught in time loop at a rural getaway. 

	“It’s not easy to blend comedy and fantasy,” says García Ropero. “Berto likes this mix of different genres and ‘5 More Minutes’ is a magnificent example.”

	“Using the conventions of genre to subvert them, reshape them, and lead audiences to places other than where they expect to go is, to me, a fascinating way of telling stories,” adds Berto Romero.

	With “Beyond Society,” Netflix is in business with a top-tier creative Spanish creative.

	Created by Spain‘s high-grossing director, J.A. Bayona, and Carles Torrens, “Beyond Society,” a three-part nonfiction follow-up to “Society of the Snow,” also underscores the fluid migration between film and TV of many of Spain’s top cineastes. The doc series seeks narrative and emotional closure for Bayona and the cast of the film as they visit the scene of the 1972 Andes Flight 571 crash, subject of the narrative feature “Society of the Snow.” 

	“It was there that we realized just how closely the true story and the people who lived through the tragedy were already intertwined with the fictional characters we had created,” Bayona has commented. “Beyond Society” traces the 50 years following the tragedy, giving voices to the survivors and the relatives of the deceased and how that flight forever marked the lives of a community.

schema.headline: TV Operators Power Spain’s Global Breakout as the San Sebastian Film Festival Readies Launch: ‘Spanish Cinema Has Never Been So Powerful’

title: Jesse Eisenberg’s ‘The Debut’ Named as Opening Night Film at Middleburg Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Jesse Eisenberg‘s “The Debut” will open the Middleburg Film Festival. A Q&A will follow with the film’s star Julianne Moore and Eisenberg.

	“The De
body:
Jesse Eisenberg‘s “The Debut” will open the Middleburg Film Festival. A Q&A will follow with the film’s star Julianne Moore and Eisenberg.

	“The Debut” follows Moore as Mona Friedman, a housewife who lands a small role in a community theater production and transforms into a zealous method actor willing to do anything to protect the artistic integrity of her part.

	The centerpiece film of the festival is “I Play Rocky,” directed by Peter Farrelly. Inspired by the true story behind the making of the 1976 film “Rocky,” Farrelly’s take stars Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone as he struggles to get his screenplay made while refusing to let go of his dream of playing the role himself. Jay Duplass and PJ Byrne will also be in attendance from the film.
	

	Léa Seydoux, Jordan Firstman, Daniel Pemberton, Jack O’Connell, Nadia Stacey are among the festival’s honorees.


	Seydoux will receive the Outstanding Achievement in Acting Award for her performance in “Gentle Monster.” Jordan Firstman will be recognized with the Breakthrough Filmmaker Award for his feature directorial debut “Club Kid,” which he wrote, directed and stars in. Composer Daniel Pemberton will receive the Distinguished Composer Award recognizing his work on “Project Hail Mary” and “Ink.” Jack O’Connell will receive the Spotlight Actor Award for his performance in “Ink.”

	Olivia Colman will attend the festival representing both “Elsinore” and “Wicker.” The Oscar-winning actress will participate in Q&As for both films. “Elsinore’s” makeup and hair designer Stacey will be presented with the festival’s Distinguished Makeup & Hair Design Award.
	

	As previously announced, “The Odyssey” artisans — costume designer Ellen Mirojnick, production designer Ruth de Jong and editor Jennifer Lame — are set to receive the Variety Creative Collaborators award.

	The conversation will be moderated by Variety’s senior artisans editor, Jazz Tangcay, on Oct. 16. The talk will look at their collaboration and serve as a career retrospective.

	The festival is set to run Oct. 15-18.

	At the festival, Tangcay and Variety’s chief awards editor, Clayton Davis will also host their annual Coffee and Contenders conversation on the state of the awards race.

schema.headline: Jesse Eisenberg’s ‘The Debut’ Named as Opening Night Film at Middleburg Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Sony Music, Universal Music Group Sue Suno Over Label-Backed Model: ‘Fruit of the Same Poisoned Tree’
description:
Sony Music Entertainment and Universal Music Group have a new grievance with AI start-up Suno.

	The two music companies on Friday filed a new, 45-p
body:
Sony Music Entertainment and Universal Music Group have a new grievance with AI start-up Suno.

	The two music companies on Friday filed a new, 45-page lawsuit in the U.S. District Court in the District of Massachusetts against the AI music-generation company, alleging Suno’s new model, backed by several other music companies, still infringe Sony Music and UMG’s copyrighted works. The two (along with some of their respective imprints, named as fellow plaintiffs) alleged Suno’s admission that its new “v6” family of models trained upon the outputs of its previous models meant that, despite the company’s claims that its new models do not infringe on copyrighted works, “training a ‘new’ model on the outputs of an infringing model does not eliminate the infringement; it launders it.”
	

	“V6 is not a fresh start; it is the fruit of the same poisoned tree,” the labels claimed.


	The lawsuit comes more than two years after the labels, together with Warner Music Group, sued Suno over allegedly training its AI models on the companies’ tracks without permission. 

	Suno did not have an immediate comment on the latest lawsuit. Suno has admitted it scraped data from publicly available resources, including YouTube, Deezer and more, though company executives have claimed its training metadata does not include artists’ names, cannot replicate material it was trained on and that Suno was increasingly trying to improve impersonation detection. Still, the labels claimed in the new suit, the deals reflect an admission by Suno that a market exists for licensing labels’ work, even as the company claims in court its training of its initial models adhered to the “fair use” doctrine.
	

	The complaint also puts a number to the recordings Sony Music and UMG allege Suno infringed: 60,202, a total the labels claimed “remain only a small portion” of the overall works violated.

	Since the initial suit in June 2024, WMG, BMG and Believe each have signed deals with Suno to license their content, which helped power the “v6” models unveiled last week.

	In the label-backed licensing announcement, Suno claimed all past models of its product that trained on unlicensed data — those that spurred such lawsuits — would no longer be supported. But Sony Music and UMG claimed that, because the new family of models is partially built on users’ outputs derived from those former models, they remain in violation of the labels’ copyrighted works.

	“It is a product of those tainted models and of the unauthorized copies of Plaintiffs’ recordings that Suno retains and continues to use,” the labels claimed. “Thus, every model Suno has ever released—from its earliest versions through v6—is the product of, and continues to exploit, Suno’s unauthorized copying of the Copyrighted Recordings.”

	The new lawsuits reflect the legally mercurial nature of AI music generation and the training of AI models. Round Hill Music, an independent music publisher, sued the company for $1 billion last month, while Americana singer Jason Isbell led a lawsuit against the company last month that seeks class-action status, alleging it allowed users to produce outputs based on artists’ identities without musicians’ consent.

	UMG in particular has flexed a litigious arm against companies such as Anthropic and the music distributor DistroKid, which it alleged on Wednesday was flooding the market with AI-generated tracks that contributed to an “AI-slop pipeline.” Its licensing deals have been limited to companies that have kept their outputs confined to their respective platforms, including Suno competitor Udio and AI-powered remixing products on Spotify and the app Hook.

	The labels have asked the court to declare that Suno infringed upon their works, award them statutory damages and force Suno to pay their attorneys’ fees. 

	“The harm Suno is causing goes far beyond these immediate economic consequences,” the complaint said. “Suno’s wholesale theft of the Copyrighted Recordings threatens the entire music ecosystem and the numerous people it employs. It also degrades the rights of artists to control their works, determine whether future uses of their works align with their aesthetic and personal values, and decide the products or services with which they wish to be associated. And it propagates the destructive theory that copyrighted music is free for the taking whenever a new technology claims that seeking and obtaining permission is just too cumbersome.”

schema.headline: Sony Music, Universal Music Group Sue Suno Over Label-Backed Model: ‘Fruit of the Same Poisoned Tree’

title: Drunk Shakespeare Theater Producer Sues Amazon, Alleging Prime Video’s ‘Off Campus’ Violated Its Trademarks
description:
Double, double toil and trouble!

	The company that produces the Drunk Shakespeare-branded theatrical shows sued Amazon, claiming an episode of Prim
body:
Double, double toil and trouble!

	The company that produces the Drunk Shakespeare-branded theatrical shows sued Amazon, claiming an episode of Prime Video’s YA ice hockey romantic-drama “Off Campus” used its trademarks without permission.

	Brass Jar, the New York-based company behind Drunk Shakespeare, did not specify the amount of monetary damages it is seeking but said in the complaint, “As a result of such counterfeiting by Defendants, Brass Jar is also entitled to recover attorneys’ fees, treble damages, and/or statutory damages of up to $2 million per counterfeit mark per type of services sold, and pursuant to each type of good sold, if any, pursuant to 15 U.S.C. § 1117,” citing the section of U.S. law addressing monetary recovery for violation of marks.
	

	Amazon declined to comment.


	“Off Campus,” which is based on a series of novels by Elle Kennedy, premiered all eight episodes on Prime Video on May 13, 2026.

	In Episode 4 of Season 1, titled “The Breakup,” there’s “an extended sequence set at a fictional college ‘Drunk Shakespeare’ production, together with multiple lines of dialogue referencing ‘Drunk Shakespeare,’ without Plaintiff’s authorization or consent,” the lawsuit states.

	Amazon’s alleged unauthorized use of the Drunk Shakespeare and Drunk trademarks, according to Brass Jar’s lawsuit, “has caused and is likely to continue to cause confusion – including reverse-confusion — mistake, and deception among consumers as to the source, sponsorship, or affiliation of Defendants’ Off Campus series and Plaintiff’s Brass Jar Productions.”
	

	Brass Jar says its live theatrical productions of Drunk Shakespeare combine “Shakespearean performance with alcohol consumption in an intimate, sophisticated, upmarket, professionally staged setting.” The company currently produces shows in New York, Chicago, Washington, D.C., Phoenix, Los Angeles and Houston, and offers additional Drunk-branded productions (including Drunk Romeo & Juliet, Drunk Dracula, Drunk Pirates and Drunk Christmas Carol).

	Brass Jar said its attorney notified Amazon in a June 3 letter of Brass Jar’s “rights in the Asserted Marks and requested that the parties discuss a resolution of Plaintiff’s concerns regarding Off Campus’s unauthorized use of Plaintiff’s marks and Trade Dress.” According to the lawsuit, counsel for Amazon “responded in a letter that included an extensive discussion of why Defendants’ program did not infringe on Plaintiff’s copyright, despite Plaintiff making no allegation in the June 3 Letter that Off Campus was infringing on Plaintiff’s copyright.”

	Brass Jar filed the lawsuit against Amazon on Thursday (Sept. 17) in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, Miami Division. A copy of the complaint is available at this link.

	According to Drunk Shakespeare’s description of the show, it goes like this: “Five professional actors gather as members of The Drunk Shakespeare Society, and one of them downs five shots of whiskey before attempting a leading role in a Shakespearean classic. What follows is 90 minutes of comedy, chaos and quick-thinking improvisation while the four sober actors fight to keep the script on track. No two performances are ever the same. It all comes down to who’s drinking and what they’re drinking.”

schema.headline: Drunk Shakespeare Theater Producer Sues Amazon, Alleging Prime Video’s ‘Off Campus’ Violated Its Trademarks

title: Lily Collins Says Goodbye to ‘Emily in Paris’ as Filming Wraps on Series Finale: ‘This Has Forever Changed Me’
description:
Lily Collins has officially bid adieu to Emily Cooper.

	The actress recently spent her last day on set playing the title role in the Netflix hit “E
body:
Lily Collins has officially bid adieu to Emily Cooper.

	The actress recently spent her last day on set playing the title role in the Netflix hit “Emily in Paris” and shared an emotional post on Instagram about the experience. 

	“I’m speechless. It’s impossible to find the words for what this journey has meant to me,” she wrote. “For so many years, Emily has been a part of my life, and through every season, she’s continued to surprise me, inspire me, and challenge me.”“Thank you, Darren Star, for dreaming up this endlessly optimistic American girl in Paris who finds herself constantly outside of her comfort zone, learning to trust herself while leaning on others as she navigates her new life,” Collins continued. “I’m so grateful you trusted me to bring her to life. Thank you to our unparalleled crew, our writers, our directors, and of course our incredible cast who is now family and who I cannot imagine this without. You have made Emily, Emily. You made this world feel like home. And merci to all of you who have been supporting us over these past 7 years and 6 seasons, keeping us inspired to dream bigger along our epic adventure.”The post concluded: “I will carry this chapter with me forever. Saying goodbye feels completely surreal and bittersweet, but mostly, I feel so incredibly proud and grateful that I got to be her. And be part of something so joyful. This has forever changed me. Au revoir, Emily Cooper…”
	

	“Emily in Paris” premiered in 2020 and is wrapping up with its sixth season on Dec. 24. Along with Collins, the cast includes Philippine Leroy-Beaulieu, Ashley Park, Lucas Bravo, Samuel Arnold, Bruno Gouery, William Abadie, Lucien Laviscount, Minnie Driver and Paul Forman.

schema.headline: Lily Collins Says Goodbye to ‘Emily in Paris’ as Filming Wraps on Series Finale: ‘This Has Forever Changed Me’

title: ‘Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom’ Review: The Ovine Adventurer Returns for a Perfectly Silly Halloween Treat
description: It’s a good year for sheep at the movies, which makes it a good year for pretty much anyone at the movies: Months after “The Sheep Detectives” prove
body:
It’s a good year for sheep at the movies, which makes it a good year for pretty much anyone at the movies: Months after “The Sheep Detectives” proved one of the surprise delights of the spring, Aardman’s reliably lovable Shaun the Sheep returns to ensure we haven’t forgotten who’s the ovine OG. The third feature-length outing for the “Wallace & Gromit” alum, “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom” arrives seven years after “A Shaun the Sheep Movie: Farmageddon” — meaning, essentially, that the new film’s primary target market wasn’t even born last time out. Not that they’ll have any trouble coming in late; with its wordless slapstick once again designed for maximum accessibility, this ebulliently daft autumnal escapade is as good a place to start as any. Few animated franchises have maintained quite this level of cheery consistency.
	

	For us elders, it doesn’t feel like much time has passed at all: It’s business and chaos as usual at Mossy Bottom Farm, where the nights are drawing in, harvest season is upon us and our rebellious title character (voiced, which isn’t exactly the term for any of these nonverbal characters, by Justin Fletcher) turns mad scientist for a Halloween-time escapade, with results as wholesomely, giddily farcical as ever. The seasonal aspect is a canny one: There remains a relative shortage of quality spooky-season viewing for very small tots, and it’s easy to imagine “The Beast of Mossy Bottom” — fully on theme, but emphatically more silly than scary — becoming an October go-to for years to come.


	It’s an indication of just how much the American commercial model of Halloween has infiltrated the U.K. over the last couple of decades that this most innocently English of cultural properties is here awash with jack o’lanterns and trick-or-treat paraphernalia. It’s days before October 31st in this sleepy corner of the countryside and while its human inhabitants are gearing up for the annual “Halloween Hoedown” (again, not a combination of words any Englishman would have encountered until fairly recently), the frequently errant flock of Mossy Bottom has been proudly tending to their own secret pumpkin patch. (If you’re wondering how sheep can grow pumpkins, you’re not in the correct spirit of things.)
	

	Anyway, when said patch is entirely decimated by an elaborately staged chain of pratfalls involving the sheep’s owner Farmer John (John Sparkes), a recalcitrant goat and an expandable laundry line — like its predecessors, the new film will always find the most inspired, complicated way to build a scene, or cause one — plucky Shaun resolves to find a quick chemical solution. Armed with confidence, a book titled “Homemade Science” (the “home” and the second ‘e’ are soon obscured) and inexplicable access to laboratory equipment, he develops a rapid-growth formula that turns pumpkin seeds into prize-standard gourds overnight; when Farmer John happens across some and slaps it on his balding pate, it has a similarly lush effect on his locks. The flaw in the formula, we soon find out, is that the pumpkins won’t stop growing. Neither will the hapless farmer’s mane, soon rendering him a yeti-like village pariah. Hairy hijinks ensue.

	This is all nonsense, of course, bounding toward a steadily more dizzy climax as it barely fills an 80-minute runtime, padding out its trifle of a plot with a whisper of romance between Farmer John and a new arrival, a nameless but redoubtable vet voiced by Nina Sosanya, plus the faithful grunt work of guard dog Bitzer (Sparkes, again). 

	But the “Shaun the Sheep” films have never been about the big picture, instead functioning on a joke-to-joke basis with an inordinately high hit rate. While the tone may often feel blithely throwaway, the filmmaking is never careless. With feature first-timers Steve Cox and Matthew Walker (both vets of Shaun’s small-screen outings) at the helm, the practical execution of the Aardman cinematic universe still amazes: Each falling-domino setpiece is a marvel of handmade detailing and methodical choreography, geed up by the delightfully frantic orchestrations of Natalie Holt’s score.

	As usual, the comedy is successfully pitched to all ages, with kids sure to revel in the generally antic energy of proceedings, while their parents can pick up passing references to “Psycho” and Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” video, among other horror touchstones, along with stray satirical jabs at parking regulations and, in a more timely touch, a wave of far-right bigotry and protest in the U.K. (In that sense, “Mossy Bottom” picks up where “Farmageddon” left off in its Brexit-era messaging about acceptance, though it would be a mistake to overstate just how much is on the film’s mind.) Everyone, meanwhile, can enjoy the simple, perfect sight gag of a voluptuous sheep cleaning a blackboard with her ample fleece. No one in live-action cinema, frankly, is doing visual comedy quite this well, each time out; to mix all manner of barnyard metaphors, when it comes to cartoon horseplay, Shaun the Sheep still wools the roost.

schema.headline: ‘Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom’ Review: The Ovine Adventurer Returns for a Perfectly Silly Halloween Treat

body:
Trey Songz
                          Alleged Sexual Assault Victim Wants Big $$$
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 18, 2026
                            11:30 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Trey Songz's alleged sexual assault victim is pleading with the court to release a huge chunk of the money the singer paid to settle the matter ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs, obtained by TMZ, Jauhara Jeffries said she settled her lawsuit in 2025 in which she claimed the singer sexually assaulted her.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She says the money is currently being held in a court-controlled escrow account until a lien issue is handled, but is asking the court to release 55% of the total amount or all amounts above $69,950.52. That means the settlement is at least around $70K, and she says she needs the money ASAP.
      

            The woman claims the delay is stopping her from being able to move on with her life. The court denied the request but set a hearing later this month.
      
    
            Jauhara sued Trey in 2021, claiming he sexually assaulted her at a Florida nightclub. She says she partied with Trey on January 1, 2018, at a New Year's Eve Party at Diddy's home and says Trey invited her to the club with other girls.
      
    
            At the club, she claimed Trey inserted his fingers into her vagina without consent. The woman said that despite the incident, she got into Trey's car later in the night.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The alleged victim claimed that during the car ride, Trey demanded she turn over her phone ... and when she refused, she said Trey had her forcibly removed from the vehicle.
      
    
            Trey adamantly denied the allegations.

            Frankie Muniz says the last couple months have been nightmarish ... implying this is his rock bottom.
      
    
            The actor-turned-racecar driver detailed his struggles in a social media post Friday ... explaining, "The last 6 weeks of my life have been a nightmare I'm praying to wake up from."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Frankie says life has felt heavy and unclear in recent days ... but, thankfully, it's caused him to engage in some real self-reflection -- to look at areas of his life that need work if he wants to continue to grow as a person.
      

            He writes, "I read that sometimes hitting rock bottom is the thing that wakes you up. It forces the changes you needed to make all along so you can live the best life possible. That idea has been sitting with me."
      
    
            Frankie says ... "In five years I believe I'll look back at this exact low point and feel grateful for it, because the high I'll be standing on then only exists because I went through this."
      
    
            Don't get it twisted ... Frankie says this isn't the end of his story, and he's not broken ... he's just being rebuilt -- and he's encouraging others who are stuck in the same boat.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            As we reported ... Frankie and his wife of 6 years, Paige Price, announced they were separating over the summer -- then the two shared a video of them dancing together after the split, which went over like a lead balloon with fans.
      
    
            It's unclear what else Frankie might be dealing with ... but, regardless, it sounds like the only way out is pushing forward.
